article_title: Creating Communities of Care: How Charter Schools Can Develop Systems That Support Student Mental Health
citation: National Charter School Resource Center, Browning, A., & Larbi-Cherif, A. (2022). Creating Communities of Care: How Charter Schools can Develop Systems that Support Student Mental Health. Manhattan Strategy Group.
title: Rocky Mountain Prep Family Advocacy Support Team (FAST) emergency family supports
description: FAST is Rocky Mountain Prep's referral-based team of teachers, social workers, and operations staff that responds to family hardship affecting student well-being. Staff with deep family relationships submit referrals; the team provides stopgap supports, including up to $300 in cash assistance for food, laundry, clothing, or other needs, while connecting families to long-term resources. Each campus has approximately $20,000 in flexible funds; in 2020-2021 FAST supported "nearly 125 families with resources for basic needs around food, shelter, mental health, and more."
requirements: Flexible emergency funds at each campus (approximately $20,000)
staff who hold deep relationships with families to submit referrals
a needs audit conducted alongside a social worker
constraints: The report describes FAST within RMP's four pre-K through 5th grade campuses in the Denver, Colorado area
target_learners: Pre-K through 5th grade students and their families
target_learning_goals: Family well-being as a foundation for student attendance, enrollment stability, and learning
examples: As of December 2021, zero students who had received FAST support had unenrolled from school
key_sources: National Charter School Resource Center, Browning, A., & Larbi-Cherif, A. (2022). Creating Communities of Care: How Charter Schools can Develop Systems that Support Student Mental Health. Manhattan Strategy Group. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED625528

article_title: A Durability and Cross-Language Transfer Benchmark for a Validated Teaching-Feedback Classification Protocol
citation: Esteban U. Vega Barajas. (2026). A Durability and Cross-Language Transfer Benchmark for a Validated Teaching-Feedback Classification Protocol. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11873
title: Reproducible balanced 45,000-comment English sentiment corpus and released build recipe
description: A released community artifact: a balanced English sentiment corpus sampled from the public RateMyProfessor research release, holding "45,000 comments across three sentiment classes with fixed splits and a fixed seed" (15,000 per class; train 31,500, development 6,750, test 6,750; mean length 231 characters). Labels derive deterministically from star ratings (positive at least 4, negative at most 2, neutral otherwise). The authors release "the build recipe, namely the script, the seed, and the split indices, so the sample is exactly reproducible, with its provenance and license stated"; raw review text is not redistributed under the source CC BY-NC-SA license.
requirements: The underlying review text remains governed by the source CC BY-NC-SA license; reconstruction via the released indices inherits its non-commercial terms
constraints: Star-derived labels are a convenience signal validated only at kappa 0.66 against human labels; corrupted structural metadata in the source means no per-institution or per-region claims
target_learners: higher-education teaching-evaluation feedback (institutional NLP use case)
target_learning_goals: classifying open-ended teaching-evaluation comments by sentiment for institutional triage and improvement
examples: Uniform per-class reservoir sampling over the full 9.54M-review file at seed 20260616, with escaped-byte decoding, dropping comments under 15 characters, and exact-duplicate removal
key_sources: Esteban U. Vega Barajas. (2026). A Durability and Cross-Language Transfer Benchmark for a Validated Teaching-Feedback Classification Protocol. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11873

article_title: Benefits of classroom remote microphone technology for inattentive children
citation: Shiels, L., Tomlin, D., Payne, J.M. et al. (2026). Benefits of classroom remote microphone technology for inattentive children. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00427-5
title: Consider referral to audiologists for remote microphone fitting when listening difficulties accompany childhood inattention
description: The article recommends remote microphone technology as a non-pharmacological classroom support for children whose inattention carries listening difficulties. It argues RMT "requires only the teacher and student to wear devices, avoiding disruption to other students' learning", and concludes that referral to audiologists for RMT fitting should be considered when LiD is a concern for inattentive or hyperactive children.
requirements: Audiologist fitting of ear-level receivers with individualized comfort-level volume adjustment
Teacher willingness to wear the transmitter and caregivers to perform daily listening checks and overnight charging
constraints: Benefits were demonstrated for auditory but not visual attention measures
Long-term use did not improve auditory processing, memory or attention skills beyond the typical trajectory
Uptake barriers such as comfort, sound quality and peer perception were not systematically documented
target_learners: Primary school children aged 6-12 with inattention or ADHD and listening difficulties
target_learning_goals: Access to verbal instruction and classroom listening
examples: In the trial, participants were fit bilaterally with Phonak Roger Focus II-312 receivers wirelessly connected to a Phonak Roger Touchscreen Microphone transmitter worn by the teacher
key_sources: Shiels, L., Tomlin, D., Payne, J.M. et al. (2026). Benefits of classroom remote microphone technology for inattentive children. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00427-5

article_title: A Meta-Analysis of the Last Two Decades of Realistic Mathematics Education Approaches
citation: Juandi, D., Kusumah, Y. S., & Tamur, M. (2022). A Meta-Analysis of the Last Two Decades of Realistic Mathematics Education Approaches. International Journal of Instruction, 15(1), 381-400. https://doi.org/10.29333/iji.2022.15122a
title: Realistic Mathematics Education (RME) as a teaching theory grounded in realistic situations
description: RME is described in the article as "a unique teaching theory for the mathematical domain" whose peculiarity is that it gives rich and "realistic" situations a prominent position in learning activities. These situations act as an entry point to explore students' initial knowledge and gradually become more formal. The meta-analysis treats RME as an instructional treatment whose effect on mathematical abilities is estimated across experimental studies, and notes game-based learning is one of its characteristics without equating the two.
requirements: Implementation uses realistic situations as the starting point of learning, from which learning gradually becomes more formal
constraints: The article notes RME's framework offers students problem situations they can imagine, which university students may no longer need
examples: Included studies applied RME across topics such as geometry, algebraic thinking, linear programming, and mathematical literacy, sometimes combined with mathematics software or e-learning tools
key_sources: Juandi, D., Kusumah, Y. S., & Tamur, M. (2022). A Meta-Analysis of the Last Two Decades of Realistic Mathematics Education Approaches. International Journal of Instruction, 15(1), 381-400. https://doi.org/10.29333/iji.2022.15122a

article_title: Students' Critical Mathematical Thinking Skills and Character: Experiments for Junior High School Students through Realistic Mathematics Education Culture-Based
citation: Palinussa, A. L. (2013). Students' Critical Mathematical Thinking Skills and Character: Experiments for Junior High School Students through Realistic Mathematics Education Culture-Based. IndoMS Journal of Mathematics Education, 4(1), 75-94. https://jurnal.ugm.ac.id/jpm
title: Realistic Mathematics Education: four basic principles translated into five classroom characteristics
description: The article presents RME, based on the philosophy of constructivism, as a mathematics instruction approach that must be linked to real-world context. Citing Gravemeijer (1994), it lists four basic principles: "guided-reinvention", "progressive mathematizing", "didactical phenomenology", and "self-developed model". These are translated into five classroom characteristics: use of context, use of models bridging by vertical instruments, students' contribution, interactivity, and intertwining, which the study operationalized as a four-step activity sequence from understanding contextual problems to drawing conclusions.
requirements: Teachers take an active role in designing teaching materials and classroom activities
Learning starts from contextual problems related to the school environment and students
examples: The study designed culture-based materials using Maluku-Ambon cultures such as pela and gandong, masohi, and sago production contexts
key_sources: Palinussa, A. L. (2013). Students' Critical Mathematical Thinking Skills and Character: Experiments for Junior High School Students through Realistic Mathematics Education Culture-Based. IndoMS Journal of Mathematics Education, 4(1), 75-94. https://jurnal.ugm.ac.id/jpm

article_title: Evaluation of the Rural Math Excel Partnership Project Final Report
citation: Nagle, K., Pratt-Williams, J., Schmidt, R., Swantek, C., Lyulchenko, M., & McGhee, R. (2016). Evaluation of the Rural Math Excel Partnership Project: Final Report. SRI International. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/projects/other/i3_ruralmath.asp
title: Rural education initiatives should anticipate technology access barriers and provide sufficient staff support and time for full implementation
description: The RMEP evaluation identifies lessons for similar rural education initiatives: consider level of participant buy-in, anticipate and troubleshoot technology access issues, and provide enough time and staff support for full implementation. The report states that "similar projects should consider level of participant buy-in, anticipate and be able to troubleshoot technology access issues, and provide enough time as well as staff support for full implementation." These lessons stem from RMEP's experience with technology delays, teacher buy-in challenges, and a short fully implemented period.
requirements: Initiatives must plan for adequate staff capacity to support participant buy-in across multiple sites
constraints: The report notes the level of direct support required by teachers and community leaders should not be underestimated, and RMEP's original staffing was insufficient at full scale
target_learners: rural middle and high school students in mathematics
target_learning_goals: preparation for advanced high school and postsecondary STEM studies
examples: RMEP staff initially tried multiple tablet technologies before finding one that streamed reliably, and the project was only fully implemented in fall 2015, which the report identifies as insufficient time for measurable impact
key_sources: Nagle, K., Pratt-Williams, J., Schmidt, R., Swantek, C., Lyulchenko, M., & McGhee, R. (2016). Evaluation of the Rural Math Excel Partnership Project: Final Report. SRI International. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/projects/other/i3_ruralmath.asp

article_title: Evaluation of the Rural Math Excel Partnership Project Final Report
citation: Nagle, K., Pratt-Williams, J., Schmidt, R., Swantek, C., Lyulchenko, M., & McGhee, R. (2016). Evaluation of the Rural Math Excel Partnership Project: Final Report. SRI International. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/projects/other/i3_ruralmath.asp
title: Rural Math Excel Partnership (RMEP) shared responsibility model
description: The RMEP Project was a rural education intervention built on a model of shared responsibility among families, teachers, and communities to prepare students for advanced STEM studies. It included six core components: a gap analysis and Math Advanced Study (MAS) guide, professional development and coaching, Family Math Nights, a project website and social media presence, community-based STEM events, and technology access. The report describes it as "a model of shared responsibility among families, teachers, and communities in rural areas for student preparation for and success in advanced high school and postsecondary STEM studies."
requirements: Active buy-in and participation from teachers, families, and community members as partners in the model
constraints: The report notes the model was only fully implemented in fall 2015, a single semester, which was insufficient time to produce measurable impacts
target_learners: middle and high school students in Algebra I, Geometry, Algebra II, and AFDA courses in rural Virginia
target_learning_goals: foundational math competency for STEM careers
preparation for postsecondary technician-level STEM education
examples: The project operated across 14 schools in six rural Virginia LEAs from 2013 to 2015, funded by an i3 development grant
key_sources: Nagle, K., Pratt-Williams, J., Schmidt, R., Swantek, C., Lyulchenko, M., & McGhee, R. (2016). Evaluation of the Rural Math Excel Partnership Project: Final Report. SRI International. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/projects/other/i3_ruralmath.asp
